summary: This informational memo gives an overview of the routing aspects of the IPv6 transition, building on the transition mechanisms for IPv6 hosts and routers.

eli5.summary: How the roads must adapt while both old and new address systems are in use.

subtitle: How networks route packets during the transition from IPv4 to IPv6.

tldr.problem: During the long transition from IPv4 to IPv6, networks must support both protocols and route packets correctly across mixed regions where some routers are IPv4-only and others are dual-stack.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes dual-IP-layer routing, static and automatic tunneling techniques, and route leaking methods that enable IPv6 regions to communicate across IPv4 infrastructure and vice versa.
tldr.outcome: Networks can deploy IPv6 incrementally and maintain connectivity across the hybrid environment without requiring every router to be upgraded at once.

facts.label: Tunneling types
facts.value: Manual static tunnels and automatic tunnels

today: RFC 2185 is an Informational RFC from September 1997 on the IPv6 transition strategy. While the transition officially concluded in 2012 and IPv6 is now the protocol for new deployments, the routing concepts described remain important for understanding hybrid environments and for historical context on how major protocol transitions are managed.

sections.title: The IPv4-to-IPv6 Transition Challenge
sections.content:
The Internet cannot simply switch from IPv4 to IPv6 overnight. During a transition period lasting years, systems must coexist: some hosts and routers understand IPv4 only, others are IPv6-capable (sometimes called "dual-stack"), and others understand only IPv6. The network must route packets correctly in this mixed environment.

The challenge is that an IPv6 packet destined for a host in an IPv4-only region may need to be converted (encapsulated) into an IPv4 packet at some point in its path, travel through IPv4 routers, and then be converted back to IPv6 at a dual-stack router connected to the destination. Routers must know how to find the right encapsulation point and route the packet consistently. This RFC, based on the transition mechanisms defined in RFC 1933, describes the routing techniques that make this possible.
sections.eli5: Some computers understand only the old address system, others the new one, some both. Messages need to be translated when crossing between old-only and new-only regions, and routers need to know where to do the translation.

sections.title: Dual-IP-Layer Routing and Addressing
sections.content:
The simplest approach to the transition is dual-IP-layer routing: routers independently support IPv4 and IPv6 routing, running separate routing protocols for each. A dual-stack router runs IPv4 routing protocols to learn routes to IPv4 addresses, and IPv6 routing protocols to learn routes to IPv6 addresses. IPv4 packets are forwarded using IPv4 routes; IPv6 packets are forwarded using IPv6 routes.

IPv6 addresses come in two forms: native IPv6 addresses (pure 128-bit addresses) and IPv4-compatible IPv6 addresses (the last 32 bits of an IPv6 address are an IPv4 address). An IPv4-compatible IPv6 address encodes the IPv4 address of a host, making it possible for an IPv6 router to extract the IPv4 address and make routing decisions based on it.

A routing region is a set of routers using the same internet protocol stack (all IPv4, all IPv6, or both). A link interface segment (LIS) is the set of systems directly connected at layer 2 that use the same routing protocol. During transition, IPv6 systems may reach beyond their traditional LIS using encapsulation and tunneling.
sections.eli5: Some routers know IPv4, others IPv6, some both. IPv4-compatible IPv6 addresses carry an IPv4 address inside them so routers can find systems on both networks.

sections.title: Tunneling and Encapsulation
sections.content:
When two routing regions cannot directly communicate because one is IPv4-only and the other is IPv6-only, packets are tunneled (encapsulated). One protocol is wrapped inside another.

Manually configured static tunnels are point-to-point links where an administrator configures two endpoints to tunnel IPv6 over IPv4 (or vice versa). Once established, the tunnel appears as a normal point-to-point link to the routing protocols, and the two tunnel endpoints can exchange routing information as if they were neighbors.

Automatic tunneling infers the tunnel endpoint from the destination address. If both a source and destination have IPv4-compatible IPv6 addresses, the source host can automatically encapsulate an IPv6 packet in an IPv4 packet, using the embedded IPv4 address as the tunnel destination. The packet travels as a normal IPv4 packet to the destination host, which decapsulates it (removes the IPv4 wrapper) and delivers the inner IPv6 packet.

Three forms of automatic tunneling are possible: (1) Host-to-host: if both source and destination have IPv4-compatible addresses, the source encapsulates and the destination decapsulates. (2) Host-to-router (configured default tunneling): if only the source has IPv4 connectivity, the host is configured with the address of a dual router and encapsulates packets to it; the router decapsulates and forwards as native IPv6. (3) Router-to-host: an IPv6 packet reaches an encapsulating router via native IPv6 routing; the router encapsulates it to an IPv4-compatible destination host.
sections.eli5: Tunneling wraps one type of message inside another. Static tunnels are like pre-built mail tubes. Automatic tunnels figure out where to send the wrapped message by reading the address.

sections.title: Route Leaking and Consistency
sections.content:
For automatic tunneling to work, routing must be consistent: IPv6 routers must be able to deliver an IPv6 packet to the correct encapsulating router, and IPv4 routers must deliver the encapsulated packet correctly.

Route leaking is the practice of advertising network-layer reachability information across routing region boundaries. An IPv6 router at the boundary of an IPv4-only region can inject routes into the IPv6 routing domain for IPv4-compatible IPv6 addresses that have IPv4 route equivalents in the IPv4 region. This tells IPv6 routers which of them should handle packets destined for systems in the IPv4-only region.

For a simple case—a small IPv4-only stub network connected to a dual backbone via one or two dual routers—the border routers can announce the IPv4 address prefix to the IPv4 domain and the corresponding IPv4-compatible IPv6 address prefix to the IPv6 domain. For complex topologies, routers may need to selectively leak specific routes so that IPv6 routing tables do not grow too large.

Once IPv6 packets reach an encapsulating router via IPv6 routing, they are encapsulated and then follow IPv4 routing paths using standard IPv4 mechanisms.
sections.eli5: Routers at the edge between IPv4-only and IPv6-only regions broadcast: "I know how to reach these IPv4-compatible IPv6 addresses." This guides other routers to send packets to the right encapsulator.

sections.title: Example: Mixed Dual and IPv4-Only Regions
sections.content:
Consider a network with Region A (dual-stack routers) connected to Region B (IPv4-only routers) via border routers R2 and R4. Hosts H1 and h2 are IPv4-only. Hosts H3-H8 are dual-capable, even though some (H7 and H8) sit in the IPv4-only region with no local IPv6 router.

When IPv4-only host h1 sends to IPv4-only host h2: the packet is sent as native IPv4 and travels entirely as IPv4, using standard IPv4 routing. Both the forward and return paths are straightforward.

When dual host H3 (in the dual region) sends to dual host H8 (in the IPv4-only region with an IPv4-compatible IPv6 address): H3 sends a native IPv6 packet. The IPv6 routing in Region A delivers it to border router R2 or R4 (which has been configured to inject routes to IPv4-compatible addresses). The border router encapsulates the IPv6 packet in IPv4, using the destination IPv4 address extracted from H8's IPv4-compatible IPv6 address. The encapsulated packet travels through Region B as a normal IPv4 packet and arrives at H8, which decapsulates it.

For the return path from H8 to H3: if H3 has an IPv4-compatible address, H8 can encapsulate and send directly. If H3 has a pure IPv6-only address, H8 must tunnel to a border router (using configured default tunneling) and let the router forward as native IPv6.
sections.eli5: When both sides of a conversation are in the old-address region, they use the old system. When one side is in a new-address region, routers automatically wrap the new messages in the old format so they can travel through the old region.
